title: Day 09 — Trusts, Protection & General Insurance Intro
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 34–41: Trusts & Life Assurance · Relevant Life · Whole of Life · Income Protection · Critical Illness · PMI · General Insurance Protection · ASU vs IPI
main_html:
IPI: own/suited/any occupation definitions; CIC: pays on diagnosis not death; ASU: short-term, covers unemployment; IPI: long-term, no unemployment

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

Protection products are central to financial planning and mortgage advice. Exam tests ability to match product to client need, understand tax treatment of premiums and benefits, and identify key differences between similar products.

34. Trusts and Life Assurance 101

A trust is a legal arrangement where the settlor transfers assets to trustees to hold and manage for the benefit of beneficiaries. Writing a life assurance policy in trust is one of the most important planning tools in mortgage and protection advice.

Why write a life policy in trust?

  • Avoids probate: proceeds are paid directly to trustees/beneficiaries — no need to wait for a Grant of Probate (which can take months)
  • Outside the estate: proceeds do not form part of the deceased's estate — potentially saving 40% IHT
  • Directed to right people: trustees ensure correct beneficiaries receive the money even if the deceased left a poorly drafted will
  • Speed: bereaved family can access funds quickly to cover mortgage, funeral costs, etc.

Types of trust used with life assurance

Trust typeBeneficiariesFlexibilityUse
Absolute (Bare) trustFixed at outset — cannot changeNone — irrevocableSimple family protection where beneficiaries are certain
Discretionary trustClass of potential beneficiaries; trustees decide who, how much, whenHigh — can add or remove within classWhere family circumstances may change; IHT planning; Relevant Life policies
Split trustPolicyholder retains benefit for critical illness / terminal illness; life cover proceeds go into trustModerateCombined life + CI policies; ensures CI payout is not caught in trust
Exam Trap: If a life policy is NOT written in trust, the proceeds form part of the deceased's estate and are subject to IHT and probate delays. Writing in trust does NOT affect the tax treatment of premiums — it affects where the proceeds go on death.
Trustees' duties: Act in the best interests of beneficiaries, not the settlor. Trustee Act 2000 gives default powers of investment. Trustees must avoid conflicts of interest and keep proper accounts.

35. Relevant Life Assurance

A Relevant Life Policy (RLP) is a tax-efficient life cover arrangement where an employer takes out a life assurance policy on an employee's life, written in trust, for the benefit of the employee's dependants.

Tax advantages
  • Employer premiums are tax-deductible as a business expense (corporation tax saving)
  • Premiums are not a benefit in kind — employee pays no income tax or NI on them
  • Proceeds paid to beneficiaries are free of income tax
  • Proceeds are outside the employee's estate for IHT purposes (must be in discretionary trust)
Key features
  • Must be written under a discretionary trust
  • Cannot be assigned or surrendered by the employee
  • Does NOT count toward the Annual Allowance (unlike death-in-service via occupational pension)
  • Suitable for directors, high earners who have used pension Annual Allowance
  • Pays lump sum on death; some include terminal illness benefit
Exam Trap: Relevant Life cover does NOT count toward the pension Annual Allowance. Death-in-service written through a registered pension scheme DOES count. This distinction is frequently tested. Also: RLP must be written in trust — if it is not, the tax advantages do not apply.

36. Whole of Life Policies

Unlike term assurance, a whole of life policy guarantees a payout on death — whenever it occurs. There is no expiry date. This certainty of payout means premiums are higher than term.

Types of whole of life policy

TypeHow sum assured / premiums workKey feature
With-profitsSum assured grows as reversionary bonuses are added; terminal bonus on deathSmoothed returns; bonuses cannot be removed once added
Unit-linkedSum assured / fund value linked to investment fund performanceTransparent; more volatile; potential for higher growth
Maximum cover (non-profit)High initial sum assured; reviewed at intervals (e.g., every 10 years); premium or sum assured adjusted at reviewCheapest initially; sum assured can fall sharply at reviews if policyholder is older/unhealthier
Low-cost / flexibleMix of protection and investment elementFlexibility to adjust cover and premiums
Reviewable vs Non-reviewable
  • Non-reviewable: fixed premium throughout life; higher initially; certainty; appropriate for IHT planning where a fixed known cost is needed
  • Reviewable: lower initial premium; reviewed periodically; can increase significantly as policyholder ages — most increases happen as policyholders approach retirement when they can least afford it
Uses of whole of life
  • IHT planning: policy in trust pays IHT bill on death; sum assured = anticipated IHT liability
  • Funeral costs
  • Leaving a lump sum legacy to family
  • Shareholder/partnership protection (combined with legal agreements)
Exam Trap: Reviewable whole of life policies can result in significantly increased premiums at review, or a reduced sum assured — the client must understand this risk. Non-reviewable (guaranteed) policies cost more upfront but provide certainty — critical for IHT planning where the liability is predictable.

37. Income Protection Insurance (IPI)

IPI (also called Permanent Health Insurance / PHI) pays a regular tax-free income if the policyholder is unable to work due to illness or injury. It is designed to replace earned income until recovery, retirement, or death.

Key features
  • Benefit amount: typically 50–65% of pre-disability earnings (to retain work incentive)
  • Deferred period: waiting period before benefit starts — 4, 13, 26, or 52 weeks; longer deferred = lower premium
  • Benefit payment period: continues until recovery, retirement date, or death
  • Long-term: unlike ASU, IPI can pay for decades
  • Own premiums paid by individual = benefit tax-free; if employer pays = benefit is taxable
Definition of disability — 3 levels
  • Own occupation: unable to do YOUR specific job — most generous, most expensive; ideal for specialist professionals (e.g., surgeon, pilot)
  • Suited occupation: unable to do a job suited to your skills, education, and experience — mid-level
  • Any occupation: unable to do ANY job at all — most restrictive, cheapest; rarely appropriate for professional clients
Waiver of premium: Many IPI policies include a waiver of premium benefit — if the policyholder is on a claim, premiums are waived. This is critical because if they couldn't pay premiums during disability, the policy would lapse when they need it most.
Exam Trap: IPI does NOT cover unemployment — only illness and injury. If a client needs redundancy cover, they need ASU. The deferred period should be aligned with any employer sick pay period (e.g., if employer pays 26 weeks sick pay, choose a 26-week deferred period).

38. Critical Illness Cover (CIC)

CIC pays a tax-free lump sum on diagnosis of a specified serious illness. It pays while the policyholder is still alive — on diagnosis, not on death.

Commonly covered conditions

  • Cancer (of specified severity)
  • Heart attack (of specified severity)
  • Stroke (with permanent symptoms)
  • Coronary artery bypass surgery
  • Multiple sclerosis
  • Kidney failure requiring dialysis
  • Organ transplant (as recipient)
  • Total permanent disability
  • Terminal illness (where life expectancy < 12 months)
Policy types
  • Standalone CIC: only pays on CI — no death benefit
  • Accelerated CIC: combined with life cover; CI claim reduces (or eliminates) life sum assured — cheaper than having both separately
  • Rider benefit: CIC added to a life policy as an add-on
  • Level, decreasing, or increasing sum assured options
Key conditions
  • Survival period: must survive a specified period (typically 14–28 days) after diagnosis before benefit is paid
  • Pre-existing conditions: typically excluded
  • Partial payments: some policies pay reduced amounts for early-stage cancers or less severe heart attacks
  • Self-inflicted injury excluded
Exam Trap: CIC pays on DIAGNOSIS — not on death. A client might receive a CIC payout and still recover fully. If the policy is accelerated and linked to life cover, the life sum assured is reduced or eliminated when a CI claim is paid. Distinguish from IPI (income) vs CIC (lump sum).

39. Private Medical Insurance (PMI)

PMI covers the cost of private medical treatment. It does not replace income — it covers hospital fees, consultant fees, and treatment costs outside the NHS.

Cover levelWhat's included
ComprehensiveInpatient, day-patient, and outpatient treatment; specialist consultations; diagnostic tests; private hospital room
Core / EssentialInpatient and day-patient only; no routine outpatient
BudgetLimited list of conditions/hospitals; lowest premiums
Underwriting methods
  • Full Medical Underwriting (FMU): detailed health declaration at outset; pre-existing conditions excluded permanently (or for stated period)
  • Moratorium: no health questions at outset; pre-existing conditions excluded for first 2 years; covered after 2 years if not suffered from in that period — simpler application process
  • Continued Personal Medical Exclusions (CPME): used when switching insurer; mirrors previous policy exclusions
Key points
  • Insurance Premium Tax (IPT): PMI premiums attract IPT at 12% (standard rate applies to health insurance)
  • Employer-provided PMI is a taxable benefit in kind (P11D benefit)
  • PMI does NOT replace income — combine with IPI for comprehensive protection
  • Group schemes (employer): usually cheaper than individual policy; underwriting may be relaxed for large groups
Exam Trap: PMI only covers treatment costs — not lost earnings. A client off work for 6 months following surgery still needs IPI for income. Also: employer-provided PMI is a P11D benefit-in-kind — the employee pays income tax on the premium value.

40. General Insurance Protection

General insurance provides protection against financial loss from unexpected events — accidents, damage, liability. Unlike life assurance, general insurance policies are typically annual contracts renewed each year.

  • Buildings insurance: covers the structure of the property (walls, roof, floors, permanent fixtures); usually required by mortgage lenders; sum insured should equal the rebuild cost, not market value
  • Contents insurance: covers moveable possessions within the home; often separately insured to buildings
  • Accidental damage: optional add-on; covers accidental damage to buildings or contents not caused by a defined peril
  • Legal expenses insurance: covers cost of pursuing or defending legal claims
  • Personal accident insurance: pays lump sum for accidental death, permanent disablement, or loss of limb/sight
Indemnity principle: General insurance operates on indemnity — the insurer pays only to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss. You cannot profit from a general insurance claim.

41. ASU vs IPI — Key Distinctions

ASU (Accident, Sickness and Unemployment) is short-term income protection covering three risks: accident, sickness, and unemployment/redundancy. It is quite different from IPI despite both protecting income.

FeatureASUIPI (Income Protection Insurance)
Maximum benefit period12–24 months per claimUntil retirement, recovery, or death
Unemployment coverYES — includes redundancyNO — illness/injury only
Deferred periodUsually 30–90 days4, 13, 26, or 52 weeks
Definition of incapacityUsually own occupation (short-term)Own / suited / any occupation (key choice)
Typical benefitUp to 65% of income; max often £1,500–£2,000/monthUp to 65% of pre-disability income
RegulationFCA regulated; historically linked to PPIFCA regulated
PPI linkPayment Protection Insurance (PPI) is a form of ASU linked to a specific credit product — widely mis-sold historicallyNo PPI equivalent
Exam Trap: ASU is the only product that covers unemployment/redundancy. IPI does NOT cover unemployment. For a client who is an employee with a mortgage and concerned about redundancy, only ASU provides that protection. However, for long-term illness risk (disability lasting years), IPI is far superior as ASU stops paying after 12–24 months.

Exam Traps — Day 09

  • Trust + IHT: Writing a life policy in trust takes proceeds outside the estate — saving 40% IHT — AND avoids probate delays. Both benefits, not just one.
  • Relevant Life: NOT a benefit in kind; premiums are corporation tax deductible; proceeds outside estate; does NOT count toward pension Annual Allowance.
  • Whole of life reviewable: Reviewable policies can lead to premium increases or sum assured reductions at review — not suitable where a fixed known cost is essential (IHT planning). Non-reviewable = certainty.
  • IPI deferred period: Match to employer sick pay period — no point starting benefit payment before employer sick pay ends.
  • CIC survival period: Must survive typically 14–28 days post-diagnosis. Terminal illness benefit may override this.
  • PMI = taxable BIK: Employer-provided PMI is a P11D benefit; employee pays income tax on the premium value.
  • ASU vs IPI: Only ASU covers redundancy. Only IPI is genuinely long-term (to retirement).

Memorise

Trust benefits
  • Outside estate → no IHT (40% saving)
  • Avoids probate → speed
  • Directed to correct beneficiaries
  • Absolute = fixed beneficiaries; Discretionary = flexible
  • Split trust: policyholder keeps CI; life goes into trust
Relevant Life
  • Employer pays, employee gets cover
  • Not a P11D benefit
  • Premiums: corporation tax deductible
  • Proceeds: IHT exempt (in discretionary trust)
  • Does NOT count toward pension Annual Allowance
IPI vs ASU
  • IPI: long-term, no unemployment, own/suited/any occ
  • ASU: short-term (12–24 months), includes unemployment
  • IPI benefit = tax-free (if individual pays premiums)
  • IPI deferred = match employer sick pay
CIC key facts
  • Pays on DIAGNOSIS not death
  • Survival period: 14–28 days
  • Accelerated = reduces life cover on claim
  • Standalone = no life cover element
  • Pre-existing conditions excluded

Practice Questions

Q1. Sarah has a whole of life policy with reviewable premiums taken out 15 years ago to cover an anticipated inheritance tax liability. At the last review, her insurer significantly increased her premium. Which alternative product would have better suited her need from the outset?
A. An ASU policy with critical illness rider
B. A non-reviewable (guaranteed) whole of life policy written in discretionary trust
C. A decreasing term assurance policy
D. An Income Protection Insurance policy
Reveal answer
Answer: B. For IHT planning, the key requirement is a guaranteed payout of a known sum at a predictable fixed premium throughout life. A non-reviewable whole of life policy in discretionary trust meets all these criteria — the premiums never increase and the sum assured is guaranteed to pay the IHT bill on death. Reviewable policies are unsuitable for IHT planning precisely because the premium uncertainty undermines the financial planning. Term assurance (C) is wrong because IHT is due on death regardless of when it occurs — term cover could expire before death.
Q2. James is a self-employed architect. He is considering income protection and wants to ensure that if he becomes unable to perform his specific professional duties, he can claim — even if he could theoretically do other work. Which definition of disability should his policy contain?
A. Any occupation
B. Suited occupation
C. Own occupation
D. Total permanent disability
Reveal answer
Answer: C — Own occupation. The own occupation definition pays if the policyholder cannot perform the duties of THEIR specific job — regardless of whether they could do other work. For a professional like an architect, this is the most appropriate and most generous definition. "Suited occupation" would allow the insurer to refuse a claim if James could theoretically work as an architectural consultant or draughtsman. "Any occupation" is the most restrictive and would only pay if James could not do any job at all — highly inappropriate for a professional.
Q3. Which of the following best explains why a Relevant Life Policy is advantageous compared to an employer providing life cover through a registered group pension scheme?
A. Relevant Life premiums attract tax relief at the employee's marginal rate
B. Relevant Life cover counts toward the employee's pension Annual Allowance, reducing taxable contributions
C. Relevant Life cover does not count toward the employee's pension Annual Allowance, making it useful for employees who have used their full allowance
D. Relevant Life policies pay on diagnosis of critical illness as well as death
Reveal answer
Answer: C. Death-in-service benefits provided through a registered pension scheme count toward the Annual Allowance (currently £60,000 for 2024/25). For high-earning employees who have used their full Annual Allowance, any death-in-service via the pension scheme would cause an Annual Allowance breach and a tax charge. Relevant Life cover sits outside the pension regime — the premiums are paid by the employer as a tax-deductible business expense, not as a pension contribution — so there is no impact on the Annual Allowance. Answer A is wrong — it is the employer (company) that gets the deduction, not the employee personally.

title: Day 10 — Business Protection, General Insurance & Mortgages
subtitle: Ch2 Topics 42–53: Business Protection · Key Person · General Insurance · Mortgage Types · Payment Vehicles · Product Types · Equity Release · Further Borrowing · Pensions · SIPP
main_html:
mortgage mechanics; equity release: lifetime mortgage (interest rolls up, NNEG) vs home reversion (sell share, no loan); pension annual allowance £60,000; SIPP — what can/cannot be invested in; UFPLS 25% tax-free / 75% taxable

CeMAP 1Ch2 scope

This day covers the final block of Chapter 2 — commercial protection, the mechanics of general insurance, and the full mortgage and pension product landscape. These are core mortgage adviser knowledge areas.

42. Business Protection Insurance

Business protection covers the financial impact on a business when a key person, shareholder, or partner dies or becomes seriously ill.

Shareholder / Partnership Protection

  • Each shareholder/partner insures the others' lives (and often CI)
  • On death, the policy pays out to enable surviving shareholders to buy the deceased's share from their estate
  • Without this: the estate may force a sale to an unwanted third party, or surviving shareholders cannot afford to buy out the share — business paralysis
Cross-option agreement
  • Gives surviving shareholders the option to buy the deceased's shares
  • Gives the deceased's personal representatives (estate) the option to sell
  • Neither party is forced — both have an option
  • IHT advantage: Business Property Relief (BPR) is preserved as there is no binding obligation to sell at death
Business Loan Protection
  • Covers outstanding business loans (director's personal guarantee)
  • Pays off the loan if the director/key person dies or suffers CI
  • Prevents lender calling in a loan (and potentially triggering insolvency) on death
  • Life cover = loan amount; term = loan term
Exam Trap: A cross-option agreement (double option) preserves Business Property Relief for IHT because there is no legal obligation to sell at death. A buy-sell agreement (compulsory purchase) removes BPR because there IS a binding obligation — the shares lose their business property status. Always recommend cross-option, not buy-sell, where BPR preservation matters.

43. Key Person Insurance

The company takes out a life (and/or CI) policy on an employee whose death or serious illness would cause significant financial loss to the business. The company is both policyholder and beneficiary.

Purpose
  • Compensate for lost profits caused by key person's absence
  • Cover costs of finding/training a replacement
  • Reassure banks and investors that the business can continue
  • Cover during a business loan guarantee period
Tax treatment (HMRC practice)
  • Premiums are tax-deductible as a trading expense if ALL four conditions are met:
    1. Policy is term assurance (not whole of life / investment element)
    2. Policy has no surrender value
    3. Cover is for loss of profits, not capital
    4. The key person is an employee or director
  • If premiums are deductible: proceeds are taxable as trading receipts
  • If premiums are NOT deductible: proceeds are NOT taxable
Exam Trap: Tax treatment of key person insurance is symmetrical — if premiums are tax-deductible, the proceeds are taxable. If premiums are NOT deductible (e.g., whole of life policy with surrender value), the proceeds are NOT taxed. Many students get this backwards. Always link deductibility of premiums to taxability of proceeds.

44. General Insurance — Principles

Six core principles govern all general insurance contracts:

PrincipleExplanationExample
IndemnityInsurer restores insured to same financial position as before — no profit from a claimCar worth £8,000 written off → insurer pays £8,000, not £10,000
Insurable interestInsured must have a financial interest in the subject matter at the time of loss (property: also at inception)Landlord can insure own property; cannot insure neighbour's property
Utmost good faith (Uberrimae Fidei)Both parties must disclose all material facts — Consumer Insurance Act 2012 requires consumers to take reasonable care not to misrepresentMust disclose previous claims, criminal convictions, property modifications
SubrogationAfter paying a claim, insurer steps into insured's shoes and can pursue recovery from a third partyCar damaged by negligent driver; insurer pays, then sues the driver
ContributionWhere same risk is covered by two policies, each insurer pays proportionate share; insured cannot recover more than the lossTwo contents policies covering same property — each pays half
Proximate causeThe dominant, effective cause of the loss (not the nearest in time) — must be an insured perilStorm causes tree to fall on house: proximate cause = storm (insured); not the weight of the tree
Average clause: If property is underinsured, the insurer applies the average clause — claim is reduced proportionally. E.g., property insured for £100,000 but rebuild cost is £200,000 (50% underinsured) → insurer pays only 50% of any valid claim.

45. Types of General Insurance

TypeWhat it coversCompulsory?
Motor — Third Party OnlyMinimum legal requirement; covers injury/damage to others; NOT own vehicleYes — Road Traffic Act 1988
Motor — TPFTThird party + fire damage + theft of own vehicleNo (above minimum)
Motor — ComprehensiveAll of TPFT + damage to own vehicle in accidentsNo
Buildings insuranceStructure: walls, roof, floors, permanent fixtures; sum = rebuild cost (not market value)Required by mortgage lenders
Contents insurancePossessions inside the home; new-for-old or indemnity basisNo
Employers' LiabilityEmployer's legal liability to employees for injury/illness at work; minimum £5mYes — Employers' Liability Act 1969
Public LiabilityBusiness or individual liability to members of the publicNo (but required in many contracts)
Professional IndemnityCovers professionals against claims arising from advice or services providedRequired by FCA for certain regulated firms
Exam Trap: The minimum legal motor insurance is Third Party Only — not comprehensive. Employers' Liability insurance is compulsory under statute for any employer (minimum £5 million cover). Buildings insurance sum insured must be the REBUILD cost — not the market value or purchase price; market value includes land, which cannot be destroyed by fire.

46. Mortgages

A mortgage is a loan secured by a legal charge on real property. The borrower (mortgagor) gives the lender (mortgagee) a legal interest in the property as security. If the borrower defaults, the lender can repossess and sell to recover the debt.

Regulatory framework
  • Regulated by FCA under MCOB (Mortgage Conduct of Business Rules)
  • First charge mortgages on residential property: regulated
  • Buy-to-let: generally unregulated (except consumer BTL — accidental landlords)
  • Consumer BTL: regulated since March 2016 (EU Mortgage Credit Directive)
Charges
  • First charge: primary mortgage; has priority in repossession
  • Second charge: additional secured loan; junior to first charge; must be repaid after first charge on sale
  • Land Registry: legal charge must be registered to be enforceable
  • SDLT: payable by buyer on purchase; additional 3% surcharge for second homes/BTL

47. Types of Mortgage

Repayment (Capital and Interest)
  • Each monthly payment covers both interest charged and a portion of the outstanding capital
  • In early years: mostly interest, little capital repaid
  • Guaranteed to be repaid in full at end of term if all payments made
  • Most common type; recommended by FCA as default for residential mortgages
Interest-Only
  • Monthly payment covers interest only — capital balance unchanged throughout term
  • Capital must be repaid in full at end of term via a separate repayment vehicle
  • Lower monthly payment but total interest paid is higher over the term
  • FCA requires lenders to assess plausibility of repayment strategy
  • Common in BTL; declining in residential use
Part-and-Part: Some borrowers split their mortgage — part on repayment, part on interest-only. Provides flexibility while ensuring some capital reduction over time. Each portion needs separate assessment.

48. Mortgage Payment Vehicles

Interest-only borrowers must have a credible strategy to repay the capital at the end of the mortgage term. The FCA requires this to be assessed.

VehicleHow it worksKey risk
Endowment policyRegular premiums build a pot; pays out at maturity to repay mortgageNo guarantee; many 1990s policies suffered shortfalls; rarely used now
ISAAnnual contributions invested in Stocks & Shares ISA; tax-free growth; aim to accumulate capital by term endInvestment risk; no guarantee pot will reach mortgage balance
Pension (PCLS)Take 25% tax-free cash lump sum at retirement to repay mortgage capitalMust retire before or at mortgage end date; pension fund must be sufficient; pension access rules may change
Sale of propertySell the property at end of term; common for BTL investorsProperty values could fall; suitable only if borrower has other residence
Investments (bonds, savings)General investment portfolio accumulated over termNo guarantee; taxation of gains outside ISA wrapper
Exam Trap: Endowment policies are no longer considered a reliable payment vehicle — many resulted in shortfalls. The FCA requires lenders to have a plausible repayment strategy for interest-only mortgages — "will sell the property" is only acceptable if the borrower has other accommodation. Using pension tax-free cash requires the retirement date to align with or precede the mortgage term end.

49. Mortgage Product Types

ProductHow rate is setKey feature
Standard Variable Rate (SVR)Lender's default rate; moves at lender's discretionNo ERC; flexible; reverts to this at end of deal; usually highest rate
Fixed rateFixed for 2, 3, 5, or 10 years; independent of base rate during fixCertainty; ERCs apply during fix; may miss out if rates fall
TrackerTracks an external rate (Bank of England base rate) + margin; e.g., BBR + 1%Moves with base rate; transparent; ERCs may apply; client takes rate risk
DiscountDiscount off SVR for a period; e.g., SVR – 1%Still moves if SVR changes; lower certainty than fixed
Capped rateCannot exceed a cap; may also have a floor (collar)Worst-case rate known; benefits if rates fall; collar prevents falling below floor
Offset mortgageSavings balance held with lender offsets outstanding mortgage balanceInterest only charged on net balance (mortgage – savings); savings earn no explicit interest but save mortgage interest at mortgage rate; flexible overpayments
Early Repayment Charges (ERCs)
  • Penalty for leaving (remortgaging) or overpaying beyond agreed limits during initial deal period
  • Typically 1–5% of outstanding balance
  • Expressed as a % declining over the deal period (e.g., 5% in year 1, 4% in year 2...)
  • No ERCs on SVR
Offset mortgage mechanics
  • Mortgage £200,000 / Savings £50,000 → interest charged on £150,000 only
  • Savings earn no stated interest but the effective return = mortgage interest rate (often better than savings rates)
  • Savings remain accessible (unlike overpayments on standard mortgage)
  • Particularly tax-efficient for higher-rate taxpayers who would pay tax on savings interest

50. Releasing Equity for Elderly

Equity release allows older homeowners (typically 55+) to access value tied up in their property without selling. Two main types regulated by the FCA:

Lifetime Mortgage
  • A loan secured on the property; most common type of equity release
  • No monthly repayments required (typically)
  • Interest rolls up (compounds) — debt grows significantly over time
  • Repaid from proceeds when property is sold (on death or permanent entry into long-term care)
  • No Negative Equity Guarantee (NNEG): Equity Release Council members must ensure debt never exceeds property value — borrower / estate can never owe more than the property is worth
  • FCA regulated
  • Optional: drawdown facility rather than single lump sum
Home Reversion Plan
  • Homeowner sells part or all of the property to the reversion company at below market value
  • Retains the right to live in the property rent-free (or for nominal rent) for life
  • NOT a loan — no interest rolls up
  • No debt accumulation, but the sold share is gone permanently
  • The homeowner (estate) only benefits from a proportion of any future property price increase
  • FCA regulated
Equity Release Council (ERC): Trade body that sets standards for the equity release market. Members must: offer No Negative Equity Guarantee, allow borrowers to move to another suitable property (portability), allow interest to be serviced voluntarily, ensure independent legal advice is taken.
Exam Trap: Rolling up interest on a lifetime mortgage can dramatically erode the estate — at 6% interest, a debt doubles in approximately 12 years. The NNEG protects against owing more than the property value, but the estate may receive very little. Also: equity release can affect entitlement to means-tested benefits (e.g., Pension Credit) because cash received increases capital assets.

51. Further Borrowing

Additional borrowing secured against existing property, beyond the original mortgage.

TypeDescriptionKey point
Further advanceAdditional lending from the existing lender, added to the existing mortgageUsually on existing or new rate; simpler process; no conveyancing required
Second charge mortgageSeparate loan from a different lender, secured behind the first chargeFCA regulated since 2016 (MCD); higher rate than first charge; used when existing lender won't lend more or ERC makes remortgaging too costly
RemortgageReplace existing mortgage with a new one — same or different lender; can also release equityFull new mortgage application; legal fees / valuation may apply; may incur ERC on existing deal
Bridging loanShort-term finance to bridge a gap (e.g., buying before selling existing property)Regulated or unregulated; very high interest rates; used in property chains or auction purchases; exit strategy critical
Exam Trap: Second charge mortgages became FCA regulated from 21 March 2016 (EU Mortgage Credit Directive implementation). Previously lightly regulated, they are now subject to the same affordability and conduct rules as first charge mortgages. Advising on second charge mortgages requires appropriate FCA permissions.

52. Pension Products

Defined Contribution (DC) / Money Purchase

  • Contributions build up in an individual pot; invested in funds chosen by member (or default)
  • Retirement income depends on contributions + investment growth + annuity rates at retirement
  • Investment risk lies with the member
  • Types: Personal pension (PP), SIPP, Stakeholder pension, Group personal pension (GPP), workplace DC (NEST)

Defined Benefit (DB) / Final Salary

  • Pension calculated by formula: final salary Ã accrual rate Ã years of service
  • Example: 1/60th Ã £60,000 final salary Ã 30 years = £30,000/year pension
  • Investment risk lies with the employer
  • Mostly public sector and legacy private sector schemes; very few open to new members in private sector
Key rule2024/25 figureNotes
Annual Allowance (AA)£60,000Max tax-relieved contributions per year (employer + employee combined). Excess taxed.
Money Purchase AA (MPAA)£10,000Triggered when flexible drawdown is accessed; severely limits further DC contributions
Tapered AAReduces from £60k to £10k for high earners (threshold: £260k adjusted income)High earners must calculate carefully
Tax reliefAt marginal rateBasic rate added at source (relief at source); higher rate claimed via self-assessment
Auto-enrolment minimumEmployer: 3% + Employee: 5% = 8% totalOn qualifying earnings band; opt-out available
Full new State Pension£221.20/week (2024/25)Requires 35 qualifying NI years; reduced if fewer; minimum 10 NI years for any State Pension
Exam Trap: The Lifetime Allowance (LTA) was abolished from 6 April 2024. However, the Lump Sum Allowance (LSA) of £268,275 (the maximum tax-free cash) and the Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance (LSDBA) of £1,073,100 remain. Tax-free cash is capped at 25% of funds OR the LSA, whichever is lower.

53. Self-Invested Personal Pension (SIPP)

A SIPP is a type of defined contribution personal pension that gives the member a much wider range of investment choices than a standard personal pension. It is FCA regulated.

Permitted investments (CAN invest in)
  • Stocks and shares (UK and international)
  • Funds: unit trusts, OEICs, investment trusts
  • ETFs
  • Government gilts and corporate bonds
  • Commercial property (offices, industrial units, retail — but NOT residential)
  • Cash deposits
  • Unlisted shares (small business investments)
Prohibited investments (CANNOT invest in)
  • Residential property (houses, flats for letting) — HMRC taxable property rules
  • Tangible moveable property: art, antiques, fine wine, classic cars, jewellery
  • Cryptocurrency (currently HMRC treats as speculative — many SIPP providers exclude)
  • Holiday property, residential land

Accessing SIPP benefits — flexible access from age 55 (rising to 57 in 2028)

Access methodDescriptionTax treatment
PCLS (Pension Commencement Lump Sum)25% tax-free cash at crystallisation; remaining 75% stays in drawdown or converts to annuity25% tax-free; 75% taxable when drawn

SSAS (Small Self-Administered Scheme): Occupational pension for small companies (often owner-managed). Unlike SIPPs, a SSAS can lend money back to the sponsoring employer (up to 50% of scheme assets on commercial terms). Can also invest in employer's commercial property. Trustee-based governance.
Exam Trap: SIPPs CANNOT invest in residential property — this is a HMRC taxable property rule; any attempt to do so triggers a 55% tax charge (unauthorised payment surcharge). Commercial property IS permitted. UFPLS means every payment is 25% tax-free / 75% taxable — different from taking PCLS upfront where the 25% is separated at crystallisation.

Exam Traps — Day 10

  • Key person tax: Deductible premiums = taxable proceeds. Non-deductible premiums = non-taxable proceeds. Symmetrical rule.
  • Cross-option vs buy-sell: Cross-option preserves Business Property Relief (BPR). Buy-sell agreement removes BPR — avoid recommending buy-sell for IHT-sensitive estates.
  • Employers' Liability: Compulsory statutory requirement — minimum £5m cover. Public liability is NOT compulsory by statute.
  • Rebuild cost â  market value: Buildings insurance must be based on rebuild cost; land value is irrelevant (can't be destroyed by fire).
  • Offset mortgage: Savings balance reduces interest charged — effective return = mortgage interest rate. Savings earn no explicit interest but are accessible.
  • Equity release NNEG: Equity Release Council members must offer No Negative Equity Guarantee. Debt can never exceed property value.
  • Lifetime Mortgage vs Home Reversion: Lifetime = loan (interest rolls up); Home Reversion = sale of share (no debt, below market value, rent-free occupancy).
  • MPAA: Once flexible drawdown is triggered, the MPAA of £10,000 applies to further DC contributions — not the full £60,000 AA.
  • SIPP residential property: Strictly prohibited; 55% unauthorised payment tax charge if attempted. Commercial property is allowed.
  • State Pension 2024/25: £221.20/week; needs 35 qualifying NI years; minimum 10 years for any State Pension.

Practice Questions

Q1. ABC Ltd pays annual premiums on a 5-year term life assurance policy on its sales director. The policy has no surrender value and covers the company against lost profits if the director dies. The premiums are treated as tax-deductible. The director dies in year 3 and the insurer pays £500,000 to ABC Ltd. How should the proceeds be treated for tax purposes?
A. Tax-free, as life assurance proceeds are always exempt from tax
B. Taxable as a trading receipt, as the premiums were tax-deductible
C. Capital gains tax applies on the difference between premiums paid and proceeds received
D. 50% taxable, 50% exempt, as the policy covered both profit loss and capital
Reveal answer
Answer: B. HMRC's approach to key person insurance is symmetrical: if the premiums were allowed as a tax-deductible trading expense, the proceeds are treated as taxable trading receipts (income). Conversely, if the premiums were NOT deductible, the proceeds are NOT taxable. In this case, all four conditions for deductibility were met (term assurance, no surrender value, covers profit loss, employee/director), so the premiums were deductible — meaning the £500,000 proceeds are taxable as trading income. Life assurance proceeds are NOT automatically tax-free in a business context.
Q2. Miriam, aged 72, owns her home worth £400,000 with no outstanding mortgage. She takes out a lifetime mortgage for £80,000 at 5% per annum interest rolled up. Assuming no repayments are made, approximately how much will be owed after 14 years?
A. £80,000 — no repayments are required so the debt stays the same
B. £112,000 — simple interest of 5% per year adds £4,000 per year
C. £160,000 — the debt approximately doubles in 14 years due to compound roll-up
D. £320,000 — the debt quadruples as compound interest dramatically accelerates
Reveal answer
Answer: C. At 5% compound interest, a debt doubles approximately every 14 years (the Rule of 72: 72 Ã· 5 = 14.4 years). £80,000 Ã (1.05)^14 â £80,000 Ã 1.98 â £158,000 — effectively doubled. This is a critical illustration of why lifetime mortgages can significantly erode the estate, and why the No Negative Equity Guarantee (NNEG) is so important — it ensures the estate will never owe more than the property value regardless of how much interest rolls up. The NNEG is a mandatory requirement for Equity Release Council members.
Q3. David, aged 58, has a SIPP worth £400,000. He has never accessed his pension. He wants to take an ad hoc lump sum of £40,000 from the SIPP today without crystallising the whole fund. Which is the most appropriate method, and what is the tax treatment?
A. Pension Commencement Lump Sum (PCLS): the entire £40,000 is tax-free as it is within 25% of the fund
B. Uncrystallised Fund Pension Lump Sum (UFPLS): £10,000 tax-free and £30,000 taxable as income
C. Drawdown: David first crystallises the whole fund, takes 25% PCLS (£100,000), then draws £40,000 from the drawdown fund — fully taxable
D. UFPLS: the full £40,000 is tax-free as it represents less than 25% of the total fund value
Reveal answer
Answer: B. An Uncrystallised Fund Pension Lump Sum (UFPLS) allows David to take ad hoc lump sums directly from his uncrystallised (unaccessed) pension pot without crystallising the whole fund. Each UFPLS payment is treated as 25% tax-free and 75% taxable as income — regardless of size. So for a £40,000 UFPLS: £10,000 (25%) is tax-free and £30,000 (75%) is taxable as income at his marginal rate. Answer D is wrong — the 25% rule applies to EACH payment, not the percentage of total fund. Answer A is wrong — PCLS requires crystallisation of at least that tranche of the pension first. UFPLS is specifically designed for ad hoc access without full crystallisation.
